title: Emergent interweaved CDW unoccupied states in hole-doping LaTe2 with element substitution
authors: Shuya Xing, Hongyu Liu, Xu Chen, Zhenkai Xie, Zhongxu Wei, Shifeng Zhao, Wenping Zhou, Xin qi Li, Zhihai Cheng
abstract: Multiple CDW-ordered layered rare-earth tellurides have increasingly emerged as a research hotspot, owing to their unconventional CDW formation, high transition temperature, and confirmed existence of axial Higgs modes. Recently, interweaved CDW in LaTe2 and its element-substituted phase LaTe2-xSbx have been investigated through TEM and ARPES measurements, revealing their distinct origins. Nevertheless, several complex diffraction features observed in TEM patterns remain unelucidated. In this work, we carried out scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) on LaTe1.6Sb0.4 crystals at 9 K. Three interweaved CDW wave vectors, q1=8/11a*, q2=5/11a* and q3=3/11a* were observed, which are induced by hole doping in unoccupied states. The q1 and q3 are theoretically verified to be nesting vectors connecting px- and py- bands. Furthermore, the satellite spots relative to the main Bragg spots p corresponding to a 11-a-superlattice have also been detected. Our findings provide critical insights for further exploring the origin of the interweaved CDW in hole/electron doping materials.
summary: This work investigates the complex Charge Density Wave (CDW) states in hole-doped layered tellurides using low-temperature STM. By analyzing unoccupied electronic states, the authors resolved three distinct, interweaved CDW wave vectors ($\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3$) and a superstructure component ($\mathbf{p}$). These findings provide critical evidence linking the emergence of multiple CDWs to Fermi surface nesting driven by hole doping.
main_problem: The primary goal is elucidating the origin of complex, interweaved Charge Density Wave (CDW) states observed in hole-doped layered rare-earth tellurides.
main_result: STM measurements revealed three distinct, superimposed CDW wave vectors ($q_1, q_2, q_3$) in unoccupied electronic states, which are theoretically linked to nesting vectors connecting $p_x$ and $p_y$ bands due to hole doping.
method: The study combines low-temperature Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) on cleaved surfaces with Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis of the resulting electronic maps, supplemented by theoretical calculations.
model_or_system: The system is layered rare-earth tellurides ($	ext{LaTe}_{2-x}	ext{Sb}_x$), focusing on the $	ext{Te-Te}$ or $	ext{Sb}$-substituted sheets. The physics involves CDW formation, superstructure development, and electronic structure mapping in response to hole doping.
key_observables: Three distinct CDW wave vectors ($\mathbf{q}_1 = 0.73 	ext{ a}^*$, $\mathbf{q}_2 = 0.47 	ext{ a}^*$, $\mathbf{q}_3 = 0.27 	ext{ a}^*$), the superstructure vector ($\mathbf{p}$), and modulation patterns observed in unoccupied electronic states.
important_parameters: Low temperature (9 K); hole doping concentration ($x$); lattice constants; nesting vectors connecting $p_x$- and $p_y$-bands.
main_assumptions: The CDW modulations are primarily governed by the filling of unoccupied electronic states, and the observed wave vectors can be mapped to Fermi surface nesting conditions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate crystal structures, SAED patterns showing multiple reflections, and STM/FFT results demonstrating superimposed stripe modulations corresponding to the three distinct CDW wave vectors and a superstructure spot $\mathbf{p}$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying complex diffraction features via TEM to performing detailed STM measurements on unoccupied states. It resolves three interweaved CDWs ($\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3$) and attributes the superstructure ($\mathbf{p}$) to covalent-like quasi-bonding (CLQB), confirming their origin through theoretical nesting vector analysis.
why_interesting: The detailed mapping of multiple, interweaved CDW vectors in relation to specific orbital character ($p$-orbitals) provides a rich playground for understanding charge instabilities and electronic correlations beyond simple mean-field models.
